description: Behind S²PACE stands the Silver family from Ukraine, united by curiosity, creativity, and a passion for discovery. Two generations, one shared mission: to turn imagination into innovation and bring forgotten space stories back to life. We combine research, analytical thinking, and Scratch programming to explore the universe in our own way. Because for us, even the sky is not the limit!
summary:
S²PACE Mars Survival Challenge is an interactive STEM-based educational simulator developed by the SRIBNI FAMILY team to explore the challenges of human survival on Mars. The simulator places players in charge of a five-day mission involving four astronauts. Players must manage essential resources, including oxygen, water, food, and electricity, while maintaining life-support systems, repairing equipment, and responding to unexpected emergencies such as dust storms, water leaks, and solar panel failures. Our solution combines scientific research with interactive gameplay. Crew consumption rates are based on NASA research, while simplified engineering models demonstrate the interdependence of energy generation, water recycling, oxygen production, and resource availability. Every decision has measurable consequences, encouraging players to balance competing needs and assess risks. Developed in Python using Tkinter, S²PACE features animated environments, interactive repair challenges, mission reports, and performance evaluation.
Designed primarily for students aged 12 and above, the simulator makes complex engineering concepts accessible and engaging. It can support STEM education in schools, universities, and science clubs by developing systems thinking, problem-solving skills, and an understanding of sustainable resource management.
S²PACE transforms the challenge of surviving on Mars into an opportunity to learn how engineering decisions shape the future of space exploration.
details:
S²PACE — Mars Survival Challenge is an interactive STEM-based educational game simulator designed to explore the scientific, technical, and environmental challenges of human survival on Mars.

Our project transforms complex engineering problems into an engaging learning experience where players must make strategic decisions, manage limited resources, and respond to emergencies.

The main goal is to demonstrate how interconnected life-support systems influence the safety and survival of a crew during a simulated mission on Mars.

How Does the Simulator Work?

S²PACE is a single-player game in which the player manages four astronauts during a five-day Martian survival mission.

The game begins with an animated rocket landing, followed by the astronauts' arrival at a Martian habitat. Players can select and control individual astronauts, move them around the station, repair equipment, and manage essential resources.

The simulator focuses on four key resources: oxygen, water, food, and electricity.

Players use an interactive Mission Control panel to manage energy consumption and operate additional systems, including water recycling, oxygen generation, and scientific research.

The game also includes unexpected emergencies, such as water leaks, solar panel damage, equipment failures, and dust storms. During a dust storm, players must evacuate all four astronauts to a safe shelter.

Each decision has measurable consequences. For example, oxygen production requires water and electricity, while water recycling helps conserve water but increases energy demand. Equipment repairs improve system performance, while emergency responses may consume limited materials or battery reserves.

At the end of each simulated day, players receive an engineering report showing resource consumption, energy balance, equipment performance, and the consequences of their decisions.

After completing the five-day mission, the game generates a final performance score out of 100 points and a mission report.

Scientific Foundations and Engineering Calculations

Our simulator incorporates crew resource consumption rates informed by research from NASA Ames Research Center.

The model uses the following approximate daily requirements per astronaut:

  • Oxygen: 0.84 kg per person.
  • Drinking and food-preparation water: 3.52 kg per person.
  • Food solids: 0.62 kg per person.

For a crew of four astronauts, this corresponds to approximately 3.36 kg of oxygen, 14.08 liters of water, and 2.48 kg of food per day.

The simulator also models the relationship between solar energy generation, battery storage, water recycling, oxygen production, and equipment efficiency.

For educational purposes, we introduced simplified scenario parameters, including a nominal solar generation capacity of 40 kW, reduced solar availability during dust storms, and a battery capacity of 300 kWh.

These engineering parameters are educational assumptions rather than validated specifications of real NASA equipment. They allow players to observe how technical decisions influence the performance of the entire habitat.

Technologies, Programming Languages, and Development Tools

S²PACE was developed using Python, with Thonny IDE as the primary programming and development environment.

We used Thonny to write, edit, execute, test, and debug the game's source code.

The simulator uses Tkinter, Python's standard graphical user interface library, to create interactive windows, buttons, control panels, animated environments, and visual representations of the Martian habitat.

The project also incorporates mathematical calculations and algorithms for resource consumption, energy balance, equipment efficiency, emergency events, and mission performance evaluation.

We developed custom 2D graphics, animated rocket landing sequences, controllable astronauts, interactive repair challenges, and original synthesized background music and sound effects.

The application runs on a desktop computer without requiring specialized hardware or an internet connection for its core gameplay.

Creativity and Innovation

The key creative feature of S²PACE is the integration of scientific calculations, engineering decision-making, and interactive storytelling into a single educational simulation.

Unlike large-scale Mars colonization games, our project focuses on a compact five-day survival mission involving four astronauts.

Players do not simply observe the mission. They directly control characters, repair systems, respond to emergencies, and manage resources.

The simulator demonstrates that improving one system may create additional demands on another. This encourages players to understand the connections between individual components rather than considering them separately.

The combination of interactive gameplay, engineering reports, visual animations, and dynamic background music makes the learning experience more accessible and engaging.

Target Audience and Educational Benefits

S²PACE is primarily designed for students aged 12–18, university students, STEM clubs, and individuals interested in space exploration, engineering, and technology.

The simulator supports the development of:

  • Systems thinking and analytical skills.
  • Engineering problem-solving.
  • Strategic planning and decision-making.
  • Resource management and sustainability awareness.
  • Risk assessment and emergency preparedness.
  • Understanding of energy and life-support systems.

Although S²PACE is currently a single-player application, it can also be used in classroom discussions and collaborative educational activities, where students analyze different strategies and compare mission results.

Intended Impact and Practical Applications

Our goal is to make space engineering more understandable and accessible through interactive STEM education.

S²PACE can be used in schools, universities, science clubs, educational workshops, science museums, and STEM competitions.

Teachers can use the simulator to demonstrate how mathematical calculations and engineering decisions affect the operation of complex systems.

Students can experiment with different strategies, analyze engineering reports, and understand why limited resources must be managed carefully.

The project also provides opportunities for future development, including more advanced resource models, additional habitat systems, expanded scientific challenges, and educational testing with students.

Factors Considered During Development

During development, our team considered several important factors: scientific credibility, resource limitations, the interdependence of life-support systems, environmental hazards, accessibility, and educational value.

We aimed to create a simulator that would be understandable to younger learners while still demonstrating meaningful engineering relationships.

We also prioritized a clear interface, manageable mission duration, interactive feedback, and compatibility with ordinary computers.

By combining NASA-informed resource calculations with simplified engineering scenarios, we sought to maintain a balance between scientific relevance and engaging gameplay.


S²PACE is more than a game about Mars. It is an educational environment where players learn to think like engineers, evaluate risks, manage resources, and understand the consequences of their decisions.

Our project demonstrates that successful space exploration depends not only on advanced technologies but also on systems thinking, responsible resource management, and informed decision-making.

S²PACE — Engineer. Decide. Survive.
